did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with a heading indicating that it is intended for musical performance, and it is attributed to David.

Did you know? The speaker addresses the Lord as “God of my righteousness” and recalls that in the past, during times of trouble, the Lord gave him relief and made room for him; he then asks for grace and for the Lord to hear his prayer.
Did you know? The speaker rebukes the “sons of man” for dishonoring him, loving what is worthless, and seeking falsehood, and he ends the verse with the word “Selah.”
Did you know? According to the psalm, the Lord has set apart the faithful for himself, and the speaker expresses confidence that the Lord will hear him when he calls.
Did you know? The verse combines restraint from sin with self-reflection: even when a person is angry or agitated, he should speak to himself in his heart and be still on his bed.
Did you know? Rather than being satisfied with outward worship, the psalm calls for “sacrifices of righteousness” and links them with the command to trust in the Lord.
Did you know? In response to the question, “Who will show us good?” the speaker asks the Lord for the “light of his face”—an expression of a request for grace, closeness, and divine illumination.
Did you know? The speaker’s joy is described as an inner joy in his heart, which he compares with the joy that comes after an abundance of grain and new wine.
Did you know? The psalm ends with personal confidence: the speaker can lie down and sleep in peace because he sees the Lord as the one who enables him to dwell in safety and secure solitude.
